title: cafaye telemetry redaction boundary
description: The rule this whole spec exists for: prompt and completion content must never appear in a telemetry span. muse is an LLM gateway, so its spans naturally want to record the prompt — 'which model, which prompt shape, how long' is the obvious thing to instrument and it is the obvious thing that writes every customer's content into a searchable, retained, widely-readable log store. PLAN.md §7b puts enforcement at the OTel collector as one chokepoint, with per-service allowlists as defence in depth, and this schema is what makes that claim checkable rather than architectural: it declares WHERE enforcement lives, WHAT may be recorded about an LLM call, and WHAT may never be recorded, and both kit's collector config and a service's own SDK setup are checked against it. The default is deny. A telemetry pipeline that drops an attribute it does not recognise is the only shape of this control that survives a well-meaning change made six months from now by someone who did not read this file — which is the realistic way this leaks, not an attacker. The house canary is muse/tests/test_trace_propagation.py, which places a unique string in both the prompt and the completion and asserts it appears nowhere in the rendered span payload, separately from asserting the dangerous key names are absent; this schema is the fleet-level form of that test. See docs/observability.md and D13 in DECISIONS.md for the enforcement-point call.

version.description: The core spec this policy was written against, so a reader can tell how stale a collector config is. Same field, same meaning as fleet.yml's `spec`.

enforcedAt.description: WHERE the redaction boundary is enforced. `collector` is the choice (PLAN.md §7b): one chokepoint in a single process, auditable in one place, and a service cannot bypass it by forgetting to configure something. `service` means each service's own SDK allowlist is the enforcement point, which is defence in depth with nothing behind it. The value is here rather than in prose because a kit collector config and a service SDK setup are both checked against this file, and a policy that only says 'enforce it somewhere' is not checkable. See D13 in DECISIONS.md for the alternatives and the cost of flipping.

defenceInDepth.description: The per-service allowlists that remain in place behind the chokepoint. Two independent barriers to the same leak, because the realistic failure is one of them being removed by a well-meaning change and nobody noticing for a month — which is exactly what muse's canary is for. Never empty: a policy with no second line is a policy whose only line is the one that can be misconfigured.

default.description: Default-deny, and not configurable. An attribute that is not on `allowed` is not emitted. Default-allow would make the safe case the thing you have to remember, and the safe case is the one nobody is thinking about when they are debugging something at 3am.

allowed.description: Every attribute name a span may carry, fleet-wide. An allowlist rather than a denylist of bad names, because a denylist has to enumerate everything that can leak and the realistic leak is a name nobody predicted. A content-policy rejection quotes the offending content back, so a scrubber is downstream of the leak; a name that is not on this list never reaches the wire.

neverRecord.description: The things that may never be recorded, stated as a list so a reader can check the allowlist against it and so the two halves of the policy can be compared. It is a list of SUBJECTS rather than of attribute names: `prompt` is not an attribute, it is the thing an attribute would carry, and the test that matters is that no allowed name is about one of these. `minItems` is a floor so an emptied list is a schema failure rather than a policy that has quietly become permissive.

prohibited.description: The subset of `neverRecord` that also has a named attribute someone will reach for. The rest are prohibited by being absent. `error.message` is in here rather than only in `neverRecord` because it is the one attribute that is already on a natural allowlist — a tracing SDK adds it by default — so the prohibition has to be explicit or it will be shipped by a default rather than by a decision.

llmCallAttributes.description: The complete set of facts about an LLM call that may be recorded, as [name, type] pairs. This is the positive half of the redaction boundary, and it is here because a policy that only says what may not be recorded is not implementable: somebody debugging a routing decision needs to know what to reach for instead. Token counts, model id, latency, status and finish reason are facts about HOW a call was served; the prompt and the completion are facts about WHAT THE CALLER SAID, and that is the line. See docs/observability.md.

verifier.description: How a service proves the boundary holds, as a path to a test. A boundary with no test is a boundary that holds until the first well-meaning change, so the policy names the test rather than trusting that one exists. The house pattern is muse/tests/test_trace_propagation.py: a canary string placed in both the prompt and the completion, asserted absent from the rendered payload of every span, and asserted separately from the key-name check so truncation cannot be what makes it pass.
